vignette:
He was six years old when his father’s fists taught him that love came with a price. The bedroom door would click shut, the footsteps heavy, and the first blow always landed on his shoulders. His mother never intervened—she pretended not to hear. By the time he turned twelve, he learned to count the seconds between strikes, to brace himself, to dissociate into the ceiling cracks. That skill—the ability to leave his own body—stayed with him.

Now, at fifty-six, Detective Leota sits in his unmarked car outside a domestic violence call. The address is familiar; he’s been here before. The man inside has a history of beating his partner. Leota’s hands rest on the steering wheel, knuckles white. He can feel his pulse in his throat, a tightness in his chest that tells him to drive away. Instead, he radios dispatch and steps out.

The job chose him. As a young patrol officer, he was drawn to cases where children were involved. He could read the slumps in their shoulders, the averted eyes. He knew the exact mix of shame and defiance. Twenty-five years later, he’s a detective in the Family Violence Unit. His colleagues call him relentless. They don’t know that he works every case like he’s saving his own childhood self.

The nightmares started in his twenties, but he didn’t name them. He’d wake up drenched, the smell of stale beer and sweat in his nostrils, his hands balled into fists. His ex-wife used to shake him, tell him he was screaming. She left after seven years. “You’re never here,” she said. He knew she meant something else: *You’re never present.* He couldn’t argue.

In the interview room, he watches the suspect slouch, arms crossed. The man’s voice is flat, rehearsed. Leota asks about the bruises. The man laughs. “She fell down the stairs.” Leota feels the familiar crawl of rage under his ribs. He forces himself to breathe. His father used the same excuses. *He fell. He’s clumsy. He’s a liar.* The memories press in like a physical weight. He excuses himself, walks to the bathroom, splashes water on his face. The mirror shows a tired man with hollow eyes, and for a second he sees the boy who never fought back.

Back in the office, he avoids the file with the child’s name from last week. He hasn’t read the medical report yet. The boy is eight years old. Leota knows the signs: withdrawn, flinching, bruises in patterns. He’ll have to interview the mother tomorrow. He already knows she’ll cry and lie. He’ll want to shake her. He won’t.

Weekends are the hardest. Alone in his apartment, he paces, unable to sit still. He checks the locks three times. He replays every interview, every detail he might have missed. His therapist—mandated after an incident where he grabbed a suspect too hard—told him he’s still fighting his father. He doesn’t know how to stop. The PCL-5 score of 62 matches what he feels: constant hypervigilance, intrusive images, the way he flinches when a door slams. He hasn’t spoken to his siblings in years. They all have their own ghosts.

Tonight, after the paperwork, he drives to the beach. The sound of waves quiets something. He sits in the sand, arms wrapped around his knees, and watches the dark water. He thinks about the eight-year-old boy he’s supposed to save. He thinks about the man he just interviewed, whose knuckles were raw. He thinks about his father, dead for a decade now, whose grave he never visited.

The tide comes in. He doesn't move.
